parts: This is the same painting. Three times.
We changed one thing. Only the color.
In red, the rainy street feels tense.
In green, it goes quiet.
In yellow, it's almost a sunny afternoon.
Nobody moved. Nothing happened. And yet it's a different scene.
Painters have known this for centuries.
Scientists have spent decades trying to measure it.
Today: what color really does to a scene, and which of the famous claims about color and your mind actually hold up.
We'll test it on famous pictures. A cathedral, a café, a bedroom, a wave, a girl, a bridge.
Some you'll see as the painter left them. Some we changed on purpose, and we'll always tell you which.
In eighteen ninety two, Claude Monet rented a room across from the cathedral in Rouen.
He painted its front. Then he painted it again.
And again. About thirty times.
Morning. Noon. Grey weather. Full sun.
The stone never changed.
The light did, and the color with it.
In the morning views the stone turns blue. In full sun, it burns gold.
Twenty of them hung together in Paris in eighteen ninety five.
Same building, twenty different buildings.
In eighteen eighty eight, in the south of France, Vincent van Gogh painted a café at night.
Blood red walls. A green ceiling. A yellow lamp glow.
That week he wrote to his brother Theo.
He said he had tried to express, with red and green, the terrible passions of humanity.
That's not a scientist talking. It's a painter telling you exactly what he aimed for.
Watch what happens if we take his red away.
The same room turns cold. Almost calm.
Put the red back, and the tension returns.
Now go east. Japan, around eighteen thirty.
Katsushika Hokusai makes a print of a giant wave about to crash over three boats.
Look at the blue.
Part of it was an imported pigment, called Prussian blue.
Scientists at the Metropolitan Museum in New York studied the print with light.
The printers didn't just swap the old blue for the new one.
They layered it with indigo, the traditional, duller blue.
Now watch the same wave in red.
It stops being the sea. It looks like fire. Or a warning.
Back to blue, and it's water again.
Same lines. Same boats. Same mountain. The color tells you what the shape is.
Van Gogh collected Japanese prints like this one. And about five weeks after the café, he painted the opposite room.
His own bedroom, in Arles.
He described it to Theo, color by color.
Pale violet walls. Red tiles. A yellow bed. A scarlet blanket. A green window.
This time, he wrote, the color had to do the work.
He wanted the room to suggest rest, or sleep.
He even left out the shadows, he said, like in Japanese prints.
Two rooms. Same painter. Same year. One built for passion, one built for rest.
Did it work on you? That part, nobody can measure.
But watch the same bedroom with every wall painted red.
It stops looking like a place to sleep.
Put the violet back, and the room settles down.
Let's try it on something ordinary.
One umbrella. Red.
Now your eye goes straight to it.
Green, and it melts into the street.
Color doesn't just decorate a scene. It decides where you look first.
Some painters paid a fortune for one color.
In Delft, around sixteen sixty five, Johannes Vermeer painted a girl with a pearl earring.
Her headscarf is ultramarine.
In the seventeenth century, it was by far the most expensive blue a painter could buy.
It was made from a stone, lapis lazuli.
In twenty eighteen, a team at the Mauritshuis in The Hague scanned the painting.
They found Vermeer used that blue most generously in the headscarf.
And they found something else. The dark background holds a green glaze.
Today it looks almost black.
Here's a rough guess at it in green. Not a restoration. Just a test.
Same girl. Same pearl. A different room around her.
Two centuries later, in London, one painter put the color in the title.
James McNeill Whistler called them nocturnes. Nocturne in Blue and Gold. Nocturne in Black and Gold.
Not a bridge. Not fireworks. Colors first.
In eighteen seventy seven, the critic John Ruskin attacked the fireworks painting.
He wrote that Whistler was flinging a pot of paint in the public's face.
Whistler sued him for libel.
In eighteen seventy eight, he won. The damages: one farthing. A quarter of a penny.
A year later, he was bankrupt.
Now see his blue night in daylight colors.
The bridge is the same. The night is gone.
So is any of this measurable? The first real clue came from a factory.
In Paris, in the eighteen twenties, a chemist named Michel-Eugène Chevreul ran the dye works at the Gobelins tapestry factory.
The weavers complained. Some of his blacks looked weak.
He tested the dye. The dye was fine.
The problem was the colors next to it.
Look at this grey square. Same grey, on red and on green.
They look different. They're not.
Chevreul published that in eighteen thirty nine. A color changes depending on its neighbours.
That's about what you see. What about what you feel? Here the evidence gets thin.
Red helps you win fights? Only in close matches, and it faded once scoring went electronic.
Blue helps creative tasks? One two thousand nine study found it did.
Green relaxes you? Nature does. Nobody has separated the color from the trees.
Yellow is easier to see. Yellow taxis in Singapore had fewer accidents than blue ones.
Pink prison cells to calm aggression? A Swiss study found no difference at all.
And the famous percentage about color and brand recognition? Nobody can find the study.
Notice the pattern. What color does to your eyes is solid. What it does to your mood is mostly a story.
And that's exactly what the painters were using.
Van Gogh didn't need a study to know where your eye would land.
Monet didn't need one to show that light rewrites a wall.
Hokusai didn't need one to turn a shape into water.
Vermeer spent a fortune on blue, and put it where you'd look first.
Whistler simply wrote the colors on the label.
They weren't changing how you feel by magic.
They were changing what you notice, what stands out, what sinks.
Feelings follow from that. Sometimes.
Try it yourself.
Look at the red version again. Where did your eye go first?
Now the green one.
Now the yellow.
Same street. Same people. Same rain.
You just watched color change a scene without changing a single thing in it.
One more round. The wave. Blue. Then red.
Vermeer's girl. A dark room. Then a green one.
Whistler's bridge. Night. Then day.
Each time, nothing in the picture moved. Only the color did.
So color does have power.
Just not the power the posters promise.
It doesn't fix your mood. It directs your eyes.
A cathedral in blue and gold. A café in red and green. A bedroom in violet.
A wave in Prussian blue. A girl in ultramarine. A bridge at night.
None of these painters ran an experiment. Each one put the right color in the right place, and let your eyes do the rest.
Next time someone says a color will calm you down, ask which study.
Next time a painting grabs you, ask which color did it.
Symbols play the same trick. There's an eye on the dollar bill that people swear a secret society put there.
We followed the paper trail. That's the next video.
